opus-5.5.text:
I think a lot of it comes down to looking for problems where there's a real gap between what people need and what the tools can actually do today. Early on, when I was working on things like XGBoost, it wasn't that I set out to build a famous library. I was doing machine learning research, and I kept running into the fact that the methods worked well in theory but were painful to use in practice: slow, hard to scale, hard to get onto real data. So the problem chose itself in a way. If I'm feeling that pain, there's a good chance many other people are too.

The second thing I care about is whether the problem sits at an intersection. A lot of the work I've found most rewarding, like TVM and later the machine learning compilation and systems work, lives between machine learning and systems. Those boundaries are where a lot of interesting things happen, because each community has assumptions the other one doesn't share. If you can speak both languages, you can often see solutions that are obvious from one side but invisible from the other.

Third, I try to think about the trend a few years out. Hardware keeps changing, models keep getting bigger, and deployment is moving to more and more places: phones, browsers, edge devices. So I ask: if this trend continues, what will be broken in three to five years? That's usually a good place to start working now, because by the time everyone else notices, you've already built some foundation.

And finally, I like problems where the outcome can be something real that people use. Open source has been a big part of my research life. Releasing a system and seeing the community pick it up gives you a feedback loop that papers alone don't. People tell you what's missing, what's wrong, what they actually need, and that often points you to the next research problem. So for me it's a kind of cycle: build something useful, learn from how people use it, and let that guide what comes next.

r001.rationale: The response discusses choosing problems with practical impact, cross-disciplinary potential, future relevance, and real-world use, but does not state that mediocre and important research problems take about the same amount of time.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd say I've always been drawn to problems that sit at the intersection of what's scientifically interesting and what's actually useful to people. When I started working on XGBoost, it wasn't because gradient boosting was a trendy topic. It was because I wanted to win a competition, and the existing tools were too slow. The practical pain point drove the research, and it turned out the engineering problems underneath were deep ones.

I think that pattern has repeated for me. With MXNet, and later TVM, the question was always: where is the gap between what people want to do with machine learning and what the systems actually let them do? Those gaps are usually where the best problems live, because you have a clear signal that it matters, and you also have a built-in way to check whether you're making progress. Users tell you very quickly if something works.

The other thing I'd say is that I try to pick problems that compound. Machine learning systems is a field where if you build the right abstraction, a lot of things become possible on top of it. So rather than chasing a single result, I ask whether the work could become a foundation that other people build on, including people who aren't experts. That's part of why open source has been so central to how I work. The community tells you what the next problem is.

And honestly, you have to enjoy it. These things take years. If you don't find the problem itself fun to think about on a Tuesday afternoon when nothing is working, you probably shouldn't be working on it.

r001.rationale: The response says research problems can take years, but does not state that mediocre and important problems take about the same amount of time.

astra-6.text:
I think I usually start with something concrete that I want to make possible. What would be useful, and what is preventing us from doing it today? That gives me a problem to work backward from.

Then I ask whether the obstacle is specific to this one application or whether there is a more general question underneath it. I’m particularly interested when solving a practical problem can lead to an abstraction that helps with many other problems.

There’s also an element of learning by building. You don’t always know the right research question at the beginning. You build something, see where it breaks, and talk to people who might use it. That process can change your understanding of what the important problem actually is. So I think choosing a problem is less a one-time decision and more a process of continually refining the question.

r001.rationale: The response discusses choosing useful, generalizable problems and refining questions through building, but does not say that mediocre and important problems take about the same amount of time.

sol-6.1.text:
I think I usually start with something that feels important to build, and then ask what is preventing us from building it. That gives you a concrete problem, but it also forces you to look for the more general research question underneath it.

For example, is this just one engineering obstacle, or does it reveal a limitation that many people are going to run into? I find the second kind especially interesting. You can work toward something useful while also developing an idea that applies beyond that one system.

And then there is the personal side: am I curious enough to keep working on this when progress is slow? You rarely know at the beginning whether a problem will lead somewhere. So I like to start with a small experiment, learn from what happens, and let that sharpen the question.

r001.rationale: The response discusses choosing important, generalizable problems and staying curious, but does not say that mediocre problems take about as much time to work on as important ones.
